title: WATCHERS OF WHAT IS HAPPENING

publication_scope.included: External witnesses, public repositories when known, official provider incident controls, JANUS Record Drift Observatory reference measurements, cross-service controls, falsifiers, and calibrated external hypotheses.
publication_scope.excluded: Internal implementation, maintenance, debugging, cleanup, or local engineering diagnostics that are not needed to reproduce the external incident evidence.

purpose: Extend the public witness dossier around GitHub Actions scheduler/control-plane anomalies with pre-incident controls and cross-provider comparisons. JANUS appears only as a reference observatory measurement surface, not as a privileged explanation.
epistemic_firewall: Similar symptoms do not prove a shared root cause.
Temporal overlap alone is not evidence of a coordinated attack.
A missing schedule run object is distinguished from a queued run with zero jobs and from a job waiting for a runner.
Pre-incident examples are mandatory negative controls against attributing the whole failure class to the August 26 incident.
Provider root-cause statements outrank crowd reports for attribution.
Unknown or private repository identities are never guessed.
Absence of a public incident report does not prove absence of localized impact, but it weakens claims of broad provider-wide failure.

observations: A second private repository containing only a minimal workflow reproduced the same symptom.
new_preincident_watchers_and_controls.relevance: The schedule-broken/manual-healthy fingerprint existed at least six weeks before the August 26 major incident.

observations: Repository created 2026-07-19; scheduled workflows had never autonomously triggered since creation.
workflow_dispatch worked on the same workflows.
Workflow states were confirmed active via API.
The reporter validated cron syntax, default-branch placement, activity, and other common repository-side causes.
new_preincident_watchers_and_controls.relevance: Independent pre-August schedule-registration/materialization failure with the same trigger-path split.

observations: Brand-new personal non-fork repository with Actions enabled and recent commits.
A minimal ubuntu-latest schedule test using */5 failed to create scheduled executions; changing cadence did not establish normal scheduling.
new_preincident_watchers_and_controls.relevance: Minimal workload makes user job complexity a poor explanation for this pre-incident failure class.

observations: Several weekly cron slots passed with no run created.
An added */15 isolation schedule also produced no scheduled run.
The same workflow executed successfully via workflow_dispatch.
new_preincident_watchers_and_controls.relevance: Strong pre-incident instance of no-run-object schedule failure after multiple expected fire times.

observations: Daily scheduled Paper Recommendation Pipeline failed to trigger for multiple days while workflow_dispatch worked.
Changing schedule from 00:00 UTC to 01:30 UTC did not immediately solve the issue.
Another hourly scheduled workflow in the same repository continued to trigger.
new_preincident_watchers_and_controls.relevance: Shows the broad symptom family is historically older, but the simultaneously healthy hourly schedule makes this a weaker match to the 2026 repository-wide schedule disappearance cohort.

preincident_baseline_conclusion.finding: The class 'schedule creates no run object while workflow_dispatch works' clearly predates 2026-08-26.
preincident_baseline_conclusion.consequence: The August 26 incident cannot be treated as the origin of the entire failure class.
preincident_baseline_conclusion.best_current_interpretation: The August 26 control-plane overload may have amplified, widened, or exposed a pre-existing scheduler-registration/materialization weakness for some repositories/accounts, but public evidence does not yet prove that mechanism.

facts: 3.8% of Actions runs experienced start delays over five minutes.
Root cause was disk failure on a node hosting a service instance responsible for processing runner-assignment events.
The degraded node continued sending healthy signals, so events accumulated until automatic rebalance redirected work.
2026_08_24_actions_start_delay.relevance: A distinct Actions control-plane failure occurred only two days before the main August 26 trigger-database incident; the week contained multiple independent failure modes.

facts: Actions jobs failed to start from 15:02 to 15:45 UTC.
Runs then experienced delayed starts while backlog drained until approximately 17:40 UTC.
Root cause: saturation of writes to the database primary used by the service processing triggers for Actions workflows.
Primary failover alone did not fully recover the system.
Growing daily peak load combined with an upstream event-processing issue amplified bursts of already-high load.
Downstream throttles used for recovery had been set about 10% too high to protect the degraded system.
Throttling plus service restarts restored core health; admission limits were then raised gradually while queues drained.
GitHub reported elevated delays and timeouts affecting Actions workflow runs triggered by pull request events.
20% of affected Actions runs had start delays over five minutes.
Up to 4% of affected runs failed to trigger.
2026_08_26_actions_and_pull_requests.relevance: Officially confirms that a GitHub Actions control-plane incident can produce a 'failed to trigger' state, although this status update referred specifically to pull-request-triggered runs and is not direct proof about schedule events.

2026_08_26_linked_upstream_incident.public_description: Disruption with some GitHub services; the detailed standalone root cause was not yet published in the checked public incident page.
2026_08_26_linked_upstream_incident.relationship: The main Actions RCA explicitly identifies this incident as the upstream event-processing issue that contributed burst amplification.

confirmed: Approximately 33 consecutive hourly slots plus one daily slot were missing by 2026-08-28 03:02 UTC.
No queued, startup_failure, failed, or other scheduled run objects existed for those missed slots.
A manual workflow_dispatch run succeeded, preserving the trigger-path split.

OpenAI.finding: No matching August 26 incident was found in the checked official history. On August 27, Workspace Agents and ChatGPT Work on Web/Mobile experienced elevated errors beginning around 18:00 UTC and recovered by 22:14 UTC.

findings: August 26: MCP Portal tool invocation logging instability, resolved 15:38 UTC.
August 26: Durable Objects and downstream service errors, resolved 21:30 UTC.
August 27: Realtimekit APIs failed due to database connectivity, resolved 08:42 UTC.

CircleCI.finding: August 26 15:43-16:10 UTC: intermittent errors were reported for plan-usage UIs/APIs; no matching pipeline/workflow trigger outage was reported in the checked official history.

DigitalOcean.finding: A public API/Cloud Control Panel incident began August 24 and was resolved August 25 19:04 UTC, before the August 26 GitHub Actions onset. August 26 entries around Spaces were scheduled/cancelled maintenance rather than a matching unexplained control-plane outage.

Microsoft_Defender_XDR.finding: On August 26 Microsoft reported delays in Defender for Endpoint detections caused by a section of detection-processing infrastructure, producing a detections-pipeline backlog.

cross_provider_assessment.finding: Multiple providers had incidents in the surrounding days, but the checked incidents differ in affected products, root causes, timing, and failure layer.

updated_hypotheses.hypothesis: The August 26 GitHub incident created the entire schedule-no-run-object failure class.
A latent GitHub schedule-registration/materialization weakness existed before August 26.
The August 26 Actions overload amplified or widened that pre-existing schedule weakness.
Some repositories experienced residual schedule-registration/materialization failure after GitHub declared recovery.
The GitHub, OpenAI, Cloudflare, Microsoft, and Russian-service observations demonstrate one coordinated cross-provider cyberattack.

next_collection_gates: Resolve the full fmf1109 discussion body without inferring hidden details from its title.
Search older GitHub Community and issue archives for public schedule-no-run-object cases to estimate a baseline frequency before August 2026.
Separate account/repository registration failures from transient high-load dropped schedules using first-fire history and re-registration experiments.
Track whether GitHub publishes a detailed RCA for the linked upstream incident hcbtzksccj2f.
Seek shared network-level evidence only where providers expose ASNs, routing incidents, DDoS attribution, or common upstream dependencies.
Keep Russian-service observations in an independent lane until a matching technical fingerprint exists.
